t: What finance is: money, time and risk
s: F00 · Finance studies how people, businesses and governments raise, allocate and manage money over time, under uncertainty. Learn why a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, how to move an amount forward or back in time, how to put a number on an uncertain outcome, and where finance does its work.
x: Finance Time value of money Interest rate Compounding Future value Present value Discounting Discount rate Risk Expected value Risk aversion Risk premium Risk-free rate Personal finance Corporate finance Investment finance Public finance Investment decision Capital budgeting Financing decision Financial system Define finance and explain why time and risk sit at the centre of almost every financial decision. Calculate the future value of an amount today and the present value of an amount received later, over whole years. Calculate the expected value of a simple uncertain outcome and explain a risk premium as compensation for bearing risk. Distinguish personal, corporate, investment and public finance by who makes the decisions and what they decide. Describe the three financial decisions every firm makes and the role finance plays in an economy.

s: F00 · Accounting records what has happened, economics explains how people and whole economies behave, and finance decides what to do next with money. Learn what each field asks of the same decision, how finance turns accounting records into forecasts, and what people in each field do.
x: Accounting Economics Scarcity Microeconomics Macroeconomics Inflation Opportunity cost Financial statements Financial accounting Managerial accounting Cash flow Depreciation Accounting profit Operating cash flow Economic profit Controller CPA CFO Distinguish finance, accounting and economics by the question each asks, the period it looks at and what it produces. Distinguish financial accounting from managerial accounting by their users, rules and purpose. Distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics and identify the economic conditions that matter to a financial decision. Explain how finance uses accounting data, and calculate accounting profit, operating cash flow and economic profit for a simple business. Apply all three perspectives to one business decision and describe typical careers in each field.

s: F00 · Almost every financial decision, from a household budget to a company’s biggest investment, rests on six principles: time value, risk and return, cash over profit, incremental cash flows, diversification and no arbitrage. Learn what each says, why it holds, and how to apply it to Ana’s first decisions about Lantern.
x: Incremental cash flow Sunk cost Sunk cost fallacy Diversification Unsystematic risk Systematic risk Law of one price Arbitrage State the six principles of financial decision-making and explain the reasoning behind each. Apply the time value of money and the trade-off between risk and return to compare choices. Distinguish cash flow from accounting profit and explain how a profitable business can run short of cash. Identify the incremental cash flows of a decision, including opportunity costs, and exclude sunk costs and unchanged costs. Explain how diversification reduces risk and why it cannot remove risk that affects the whole economy. Explain the law of one price and calculate the profit from a simple arbitrage.

s: F00 · Where a business’s money comes from (debt and equity), and whether it can pay its bills when they fall due. Learn the words professionals use for both, calculate working capital and the current ratio, and see why a business can be worth a lot and still run out of cash.
x: Capital Debt Equity Interest Principal Default Cost of capital Capital structure Leverage Debt-to-equity ratio Liquidity Solvency Emergency fund Current assets Current liabilities Working capital Current ratio Quick ratio Define capital and distinguish debt from equity by the claim each gives, the risk each carries and what each costs a business in principle. Explain why debt magnifies the returns to shareholders in both good years and bad. Distinguish the liquidity of an asset from the liquidity of a firm, and liquidity from solvency. Calculate working capital, the current ratio and the quick ratio, and interpret what they do and do not show. Assess the liquidity of a person or a small business, including Ana’s emergency fund.

s: F00 · Book value, market value, market capitalisation, enterprise value, EBITDA and the multiples built from them: the words analysts use to say what a company is worth. Learn to calculate each one for Harbourline Roasters, to say what it leaves out, and to see why every valuation rests on assumptions.
x: Valuation Book value of equity Market value Market capitalisation Market-to-book ratio Enterprise value Net debt EBIT D&A Amortisation EBITDA Valuation multiple EV/EBITDA Earnings per share P/E ratio Distinguish book value from market value, and explain why the two usually differ. Calculate market capitalisation and enterprise value, and explain why enterprise value adds debt and subtracts cash. Calculate EBIT and EBITDA from an income statement, and explain what EBITDA leaves out. Calculate and interpret the EV/EBITDA and P/E multiples, matching each numerator with the right measure of earnings. Estimate a value range from peer multiples and explain how the result depends on the assumptions chosen.

s: F00 · Interest is what money earns over time; inflation is what time takes away. Learn simple and compound interest, why compounding frequency matters, how an APR differs from an effective annual rate, and how to turn a nominal return into a real one, so you can tell whether savings are really growing.
x: Simple interest Compound interest Compounding frequency Effective annual rate APR Annual percentage yield Inflation Price index Consumer Price Index Purchasing power Nominal return Real return Real interest rate Calculate simple and compound interest, and explain why compounding makes balances grow faster over time. Calculate future values with more than one compounding period a year, and convert a quoted annual rate into an effective annual rate. Distinguish an APR (a quoted annual rate) from an effective annual rate, and compare two rates quoted on different bases. Explain inflation and purchasing power, and calculate an inflation rate from a price index. Calculate a real return exactly and by approximation, and recognise when the approximation fails.

s: F00 · Financial markets move savings to the people and firms who can put them to work, set prices for risk and time, and let investors sell when they need cash. Learn the main ways to sort them: direct or through an intermediary, new issues or resale, short or long term, what is traded, and where.
x: Financial market Financial assets Security Issuer Price discovery Liquidity Direct finance Indirect finance Financial intermediary Interest-rate spread Primary market Initial public offering Secondary market Money market Capital market Equity market Bond market Bond Foreign-exchange market Commodity market Derivatives market Hedging Exchange Over-the-counter market Explain the four jobs financial markets do: channelling savings to investment, discovering prices, providing liquidity and sharing risk. Distinguish direct finance from indirect finance, and calculate an intermediary’s interest-rate spread. Classify a transaction as primary or secondary, and an instrument as belonging to the money market or the capital market. Describe what is traded in equity, bond, foreign-exchange, commodity and derivatives markets, and convert an amount between currencies. Compare exchanges with over-the-counter markets.

s: F00 · Banks, investment banks, pension funds, insurers, mutual funds, hedge funds, brokers and dealers each do a different job in moving money and risk, and central banks and regulators set the rules they work under. Learn who does what, how each is paid, and what the protections such as deposit insurance do and do not cover.
x: Commercial bank Bank run Investment bank Underwriting Underwriting spread Net proceeds Lock-up Institutional investors Pension fund Mutual fund Exchange-traded fund Net asset value Hedge fund Leverage Short selling Broker Dealer Market maker Bid Ask Bid-ask spread Federal Reserve SEC FDIC Ownership category Identify households, firms and governments as savers and borrowers, and describe the job of each kind of financial institution. Distinguish commercial banks from investment banks, and brokers from dealers and market makers. Compare pension funds, insurance companies, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds and hedge funds by whose money they manage and how investors get it back. Calculate a bid-ask spread, the net proceeds of a share offering and a fund’s net asset value per share. Describe what the Federal Reserve, the SEC, FINRA, the CFTC and the FDIC do, and calculate how much of a deposit FDIC insurance covers.

s: F00 · When the people who run a business are not the people who own it or lend to it, their interests can pull apart. Learn why that happens, what it costs, and the tools (boards, incentive pay, loan covenants, disclosure) used to keep managers working for the people whose money they use.
x: Separation of ownership and control Principal Agent Agency problem Agency costs Risk shifting Covenants Board of directors Incentive pay Stock options Shareholder view Stakeholder view Explain the separation of ownership and control and the principal-agent relationship it creates. Identify the main conflicts between shareholders and managers and between shareholders and lenders. Calculate how a manager’s ownership stake changes who bears the cost of a perk, and how risk-shifting moves value from lenders to shareholders. Describe what a board of directors does and evaluate incentive pay, including its side effects. Compare the shareholder and stakeholder views of what a company is for. Apply loan covenants and governance tools to Lantern Coffee as it takes on outside investors and debt.

t: What accounting is and why businesses need it
s: F01 · Accounting turns what happens to a business into information that owners, lenders, investors and governments can act on. Learn who relies on that information, the four statements it produces, who writes the rules, and the concepts that make the numbers worth trusting.
x: Accounting Financial accounting Managerial accounting Tax accounting GAAP IFRS FASB IASB SEC Conceptual framework Relevance Materiality Faithful representation Economic entity assumption Going concern assumption Monetary unit assumption Time period assumption Historical cost principle Full disclosure principle Financial statements Audit Explain accounting as an information system that identifies, records and communicates the economic events of a business. Identify the main users of accounting information and the decisions each one makes with it. Distinguish financial, managerial and tax accounting by their users, rules and purpose. Describe the question each of the four financial statements answers. Explain who sets accounting standards in the United States and internationally, and what the conceptual framework is for. Apply the qualitative characteristics, the four basic assumptions and the basic principles to everyday reporting decisions.

s: F01 · An account is where a business keeps every increase and decrease in one item. Learn the five kinds of account, how accounts are grouped as current or noncurrent and as permanent or temporary, and how a chart of accounts organises them.
x: Account Asset Liability Equity Revenue Expense Current asset Noncurrent asset Current liability Noncurrent liability Operating cycle Contra account Chart of accounts Permanent account Temporary account Common stock Explain what an account is and why a business keeps a separate account for each item it tracks. Classify accounts as assets, liabilities, equity, revenue or expenses, using the definitions in the FASB and IASB conceptual frameworks. Classify assets and liabilities as current or noncurrent, and accounts as permanent or temporary. Explain how a contra account works, using accumulated depreciation as the example. Read and extend a chart of accounts, recognising the US and IFRS or UK names for the same items. Justify the classification of borderline items such as prepaid insurance, unearned revenue and the current portion of a loan.

s: F01 · Every business’s resources come from creditors or owners, so assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Learn to trace any transaction through that equation and to see how revenue, expenses and dividends change what the owners own.
x: Accounting equation Net assets Dual aspect Unearned revenue Contributed capital Retained earnings Dividends Net income Expanded accounting equation Executory contract State the accounting equation and explain why it must balance after every transaction. Analyse a business transaction into its effects on assets, liabilities and equity. Use the expanded accounting equation to show how revenue, expenses and dividends change equity. Distinguish contributed capital from retained earnings. Calculate a missing element of the equation, including net income, from beginning and ending balances.

s: F01 · Debit means the left side of an account and credit means the right, nothing more. Work out from the accounting equation which side increases each kind of account, read normal balances, and calculate the balance of any T-account.
x: Debit Credit T-account Normal balance Double-entry bookkeeping Account balance Explain what debit and credit mean in bookkeeping, and why neither means good or bad. Explain, from the accounting equation, why each kind of account increases on the side it does. State the normal balance of assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses, dividends and contra-asset accounts. Calculate the balance of a T-account, and find a missing figure from the other three. Interpret a bank statement’s debits and credits from the bank’s point of view.

s: F01 · Every entry starts with a document and ends with a balanced record. Decide whether an event belongs in the books, analyse it in five steps, and write it in general journal form, including entries with more than two lines.
x: Source document Journal General journal Journal entry Compound entry Journalising Transaction analysis Identify the source document behind a transaction, and decide whether an event should be recorded at all. Analyse a transaction in five steps, from naming the accounts to checking that debits equal credits. Record simple and compound entries in general journal format, with dates, indented credits and explanations. Journalise Lantern Coffee’s March transactions. Diagnose common journalising errors, including the ones a balanced entry can hide.

s: F01 · The journal tells the story in date order; the general ledger sorts the same amounts by account so that every balance can be read. Learn to post each journal line, cross-reference the two records so any amount can be traced, keep running balances, and check customer and supplier detail against its control account.
x: General ledger Posting Posting reference Balance-column account Subsidiary ledger Control account Explain why a business keeps both a journal and a general ledger, and what each is for. Post journal entries to ledger accounts, writing posting references in both the journal and the ledger. Calculate an account’s balance in T-account form and in balance-column (running-balance) form. Reconcile a subsidiary ledger of customers or suppliers with its control account. Trace an amount between the ledger and the journal, and locate common posting errors. Distinguish what accounting software does automatically from the judgements it leaves to people.

s: F01 · List every ledger balance in a debit or a credit column and the two totals should agree. Learn to prepare a trial balance, to use the gap between the totals to track down mistakes, and to recognise the errors that a trial balance in perfect balance can still hide.
x: Trial balance Unadjusted trial balance Transposition error Slide error Compensating error Error of omission Error of commission Error of principle Error of original entry Reversal of entries Prepare a trial balance from ledger balances, listing accounts in chart order with each balance in its debit or credit column. Explain why the two columns must agree, and what a balancing trial balance does and does not prove. Identify errors a trial balance cannot detect: omissions, wrong accounts, reversals, compensating errors, and entries recorded twice or at the same wrong amount on both sides. Locate an error from the difference between the column totals, using the halving test and the test for divisibility by 9. Distinguish the unadjusted, adjusted and post-closing trial balances, and explain why none of them is a financial statement.

s: F01 · Profit and cash run on different clocks. Learn when revenue and expenses belong to a period under the accrual basis, how that differs from the cash basis, and how deferrals and accruals set up the month-end adjustments.
x: Cash basis Accrual basis Revenue recognition principle Expense recognition principle Performance obligation Deferral Accrual Distinguish the cash basis from the accrual basis and calculate profit under each for the same period. Apply the revenue recognition principle, including the five-step model of ASC 606 and IFRS 15, to decide when revenue is earned. Apply the expense recognition principle and explain what “matching” does and does not justify. Classify a gap between cash and recognition as a deferral or an accrual of revenue or expense. Reconcile cash-basis profit to accrual-basis net income item by item. Explain why US GAAP and IFRS financial statements use the accrual basis and where the cash basis is still used.

s: F01 · Some changes arrive without a transaction: insurance expires, wages build up, equipment wears. Learn to find, calculate and record the five kinds of month-end adjustment, and to prepare the adjusted trial balance that the financial statements are built from.
x: Adjusting entry Prepaid expense Accrued revenue Accrued expense Depreciation Accumulated depreciation Book value Straight-line method Residual value Useful life Adjusted trial balance Explain why adjusting entries are needed at the end of each period and why they never involve Cash. Record adjusting entries for prepaid expenses, unearned revenue, accrued revenue, accrued expenses and depreciation. Calculate straight-line depreciation, accumulated depreciation and book value, including for part of a year. Calculate accrued interest with I = P × r × t. Prepare an adjusted trial balance from an unadjusted trial balance and the adjusting entries. Analyse the effect of omitting an adjustment on net income, assets, liabilities and equity.

t: Financial statements from the adjusted trial balance
s: F01 · Turn Lantern’s adjusted trial balance into an income statement, a statement of changes in equity, a classified balance sheet and a statement of cash flows, see how the four fit together, and read what they say about Lantern’s first month.
x: Income statement Statement of changes in equity Statement of retained earnings Balance sheet Classified balance sheet Statement of cash flows Operating activities Investing activities Financing activities Articulation Prepare a single-step income statement from an adjusted trial balance. Prepare a statement of changes in equity and a statement of retained earnings. Prepare a classified balance sheet, presenting a contra-asset correctly. Prepare a statement of cash flows by the direct method, classifying each cash flow as operating, investing or financing. Explain how the four statements articulate and check that they do. Interpret a small business’s statements: its profit, where its cash came from and how it is financed.

s: F01 · At the end of a period, the revenue, expense and dividend accounts are emptied into Retained Earnings so that the next period starts from zero. Learn the four closing entries, record Lantern’s for March, and prove the result with a post-closing trial balance.
x: Closing entries Income Summary Post-closing trial balance Distinguish temporary accounts, which are closed at the end of each period, from permanent accounts, which carry their balances forward. Explain the two jobs closing entries do: resetting the temporary accounts and bringing Retained Earnings up to date. Record the four closing entries through Income Summary, for a net income and for a net loss. Prepare a post-closing trial balance and use it to confirm that only permanent accounts remain open. Calculate retained earnings after closing and reconcile it with the statement of changes in equity and the balance sheet. Identify common closing errors and correct them.

s: F01 · Every period, every business runs the same nine steps, from analysing a transaction to proving that the ledger is ready for the next period. See the whole cycle at once, use the optional worksheet and reversing entries, correct errors after posting, and protect the records with internal control.
x: Accounting cycle Worksheet Reversing entry Correcting entry Internal control Segregation of duties List the nine steps of the accounting cycle in order, and say which happen during the period and which at its end. Record reversing entries for accruals and show that they lead to the same balances as recording without them. Record correcting entries for errors found after posting: a wrong account, a wrong amount and an omitted entry. Explain what internal control is, and apply segregation of duties, authorisation, documentation, physical safeguards and reconciliations to a small business. Apply the whole cycle to a small business, from its first transaction to its post-closing trial balance. Distinguish the steps that accounting software automates from the judgements it cannot make.

t: Datasets: rows, columns, records and variables
s: B02 · Before you clean or analyse a table, describe it exactly: what one row is, what kind of value each column holds, which column identifies each row, and what every column is supposed to contain. Get this wrong and correct arithmetic gives the wrong answer.
x: Dataset Observation Variable Unit of observation Tidy data Nominal variable Ordinal variable Interval variable Ratio variable Discrete variable Continuous variable Primary key Composite key Data dictionary Wide format Long format Identify the observations, variables and unit of observation of a dataset, and explain why the unit changes the answer to a question. Recognise tidy and untidy layouts, and describe what makes a layout untidy. Classify a variable as nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, and as discrete or continuous, and state which comparisons and summaries it supports. Choose a primary key or composite key for a table and test whether it identifies every row. Write a data dictionary entry that defines a column’s meaning, level, type, unit and rules. Distinguish wide and long layouts of the same data.

t: Profiling a dataset and writing validation rules
s: B02 · Find out what a dataset really contains before you change it: profile every column, name each problem by the quality dimension it affects, and turn what you find into precise validation rules and a cleaning plan.
x: Data profiling Data quality dimension Completeness Validity Accuracy Consistency Uniqueness Timeliness Validation rule Range check Format check Referential integrity Cross-field check Profile a dataset: its shape, types, blanks, distinct values, ranges, summary statistics and frequency tables, with cross-checks between columns. Classify a data problem by the quality dimension it affects: completeness, validity, accuracy, consistency, uniqueness or timeliness. Write validation rules of each kind (type, range, set membership, format, uniqueness, completeness, cross-field and referential integrity) and give each a severity. Calculate completeness, a rule’s failure rate and the share of rows that fail at least one rule. Explain why a value can pass every validation rule and still be wrong. Plan cleaning from a profile by turning its findings into a prioritised issue list before changing any data.

s: B02 · A record counted twice inflates revenue, customer numbers and averages without any warning. Learn to tell exact copies, conflicting versions and near duplicates apart, decide what counts as “the same” for the business, and remove duplicates without deleting genuine repeat orders.
x: Duplicate record Exact duplicate Near duplicate Business key Deduplication Survivorship rule Fuzzy matching Edit distance Distinguish exact duplicates, repeated keys with conflicting values and near duplicates, and explain how each kind arises. Identify the business key that defines “the same record” for a dataset, and the evidence that separates a duplicate from a genuine repeat. Choose a survivorship rule (first, latest update, most complete or merge) for a group of duplicates and justify it. Calculate how duplicates distort totals, counts and averages. Compute the edit distance between two short strings and explain how fuzzy matching uses it. Find duplicates with a spreadsheet, with SQL and with pandas.

t: Incorrect data types and inconsistent dates
s: B02 · A price stored as text won’t add up, and a date stored as text won’t sort. Learn to give every column the right data type, convert numbers written in different local formats, keep identifiers as text, and turn a column of mixed dates into unambiguous ISO 8601 dates without guessing.
x: Data type Type conversion Locale Leading zero Ambiguous date ISO 8601 Serial date UTC Identify the data type each column should have, and explain how a wrong type breaks sorting, sums and joins. Convert numbers stored as text, including currency symbols, thousands separators, decimal commas and negatives in parentheses. Recognise identifiers that look numeric but must stay text, such as codes with leading zeros. Convert dates in mixed formats to ISO 8601, resolving ambiguous dates with evidence rather than guesswork. Calculate the date behind a spreadsheet serial number, and the serial number of a date, in the 1900 date system. Explain how to store and report times so that time zones and daylight saving don’t corrupt them.

s: B02 · “North”, “north ”, “N.” and “Nrth” are one region to a person and four to a computer. Learn to normalise whitespace, case and Unicode, consolidate variants with a reviewed mapping table, split and extract fields with simple patterns, and see how consolidation changes counts and averages.
x: Whitespace Non-breaking space Code point Case normalisation Unicode normalisation Mapping table Controlled vocabulary Category consolidation Regular expression Identify the whitespace, case, punctuation and Unicode differences that make equal-looking text values unequal. Normalise text values by trimming, case normalisation and Unicode normalisation, in a sensible order. Build and maintain a mapping table that consolidates variants into a controlled vocabulary. Use simple regular expressions to check, extract and split text, and explain their limits. Calculate how category consolidation changes group counts and averages.

s: B02 · A blank cell is a question: why is the value missing? Learn to find every form missing data takes, judge whether the gaps are random, and choose between deleting and imputing without quietly biasing the answer.
x: Missing value MCAR MAR MNAR Listwise deletion Pairwise deletion Imputation Mean imputation Missing-value indicator Multiple imputation Recognise the forms missing data takes in an export, including placeholders such as 0, −999 and “unknown”, and blanks that really mean zero. Distinguish data missing completely at random, at random and not at random, and explain why the data alone cannot settle which applies. Calculate how deletion, mean imputation and group-wise imputation change a mean, a standard deviation and a correlation. Choose between deletion, single imputation, a missing-value indicator and multiple imputation for a stated purpose, and justify the choice. Apply imputation without leakage by computing fill values from training data only.

s: B02 · Some unusual values are mistakes, some are impossible and some are the most important rows in the file. Learn to flag them with quartile fences and robust z-scores, to see why the ordinary z-score can miss them, and to choose and document a treatment that fits the question.
x: Outlier Interquartile range Tukey fences Z-score Modified z-score Median absolute deviation Winsorising Masking Robust statistic Distinguish impossible values, errors and genuine extreme values, and explain why impossible values are a validation problem before they are an outlier problem. Calculate quartiles, the interquartile range, Tukey fences, z-scores and modified z-scores for a small dataset. Explain masking and why rules built on the median and the median absolute deviation resist it. Choose a treatment for a flagged value (correct, remove, cap, keep with robust statistics, or flag) and calculate its effect on the mean and the median. Document an outlier decision so that someone else could reproduce it.

s: B02 · Order values, hotel bills and study hours pile up at the low end and stretch out in a long tail. Learn to measure that skew, to see when it distorts summaries, outlier rules and models, and to transform a variable, read the results back in real units, and know when to leave it alone.
x: Skewness Right-skewed Left-skewed Log transformation Log1p transformation Square-root transformation Box–Cox transformation Geometric mean Calculate the sample skewness of a small dataset with the adjusted Fisher–Pearson coefficient and interpret its sign. Explain how skewness distorts means, outlier rules and models. Transform a skewed variable with a log, log(1 + x), square root or Box–Cox transformation, choosing one that suits its values. Interpret results after a log transformation, including log differences as approximate percentage changes and back-transformed means as geometric means. Decide when a variable should not be transformed.

s: B02 · Put numeric variables on comparable scales with min–max normalisation, standardisation and robust scaling, so that no variable dominates an analysis just because of its units. Learn which methods need scaling, what an outlier does to each scaler, and how to fit the scaling on training data only so that no test information leaks into the model.
x: Feature scaling Min–max normalisation Standardisation Robust scaling Data leakage Training set Test set Explain why distance-based, penalised and gradient-based methods need features on comparable scales, and when scaling makes no difference. Calculate min–max normalised, standardised and robust-scaled values, and convert scaled values back to the original units. Compare how an extreme value affects each scaler and choose a suitable method for a given variable. Distinguish the different meanings of “normalisation” and state precisely which transformation was used. Apply scaling without data leakage: fit the parameters on the training set and apply them unchanged to the test set and to new data. Interpret distances and regression coefficients computed from scaled variables.

s: B02 · Turn categories such as region, room type or roast into numbers a model can use, without inventing an order or a distance the categories don’t have. Learn one-hot and dummy coding, ordinal, frequency and target encoding, and how to handle the dummy-variable trap, rare and unseen categories, and variables with thousands of values.
x: Categorical encoding One-hot encoding Dummy variable Dummy-variable trap Reference category Ordinal encoding Label encoding Frequency encoding Target encoding High cardinality Explain why most models need categorical variables converted to numbers, and how arbitrary codes mislead linear and distance-based models. Encode a nominal variable with one-hot encoding or dummy coding, and calculate how many columns an encoding creates. Explain the dummy-variable trap and decide when dropping a reference category is necessary and when keeping every column is better. Apply ordinal, frequency and target encoding, and state the assumption each makes. Calculate smoothed and out-of-fold target encodings that avoid data leakage. Handle rare categories, categories unseen at prediction time and high-cardinality variables.

s: B02 · Clean data rarely arrives in the shape a question needs. Learn to derive new variables, sort values into bins, aggregate, reshape between wide and long, and join tables, and to check every step so that it adds information rather than errors.
x: Derived variable Binning Granularity Aggregation Weighted average Reshaping Pivot Melt Join Inner join Left join Full outer join Row explosion Construct derived variables (totals, ratios, flags, date parts and durations) and use them to check stored values. Compare equal-width, equal-frequency and business-defined bins, and explain what binning throws away. Calculate group summaries at a stated granularity, and distinguish the overall average from an average of group averages. Reshape a table between wide and long format, and explain which questions need each layout. Determine the row count of inner, left and full joins, including the row explosion caused by repeated keys. Design a repeatable sequence of transformations that leaves the raw data untouched.

t: Data quality reporting and a reproducible workflow
s: B02 · Cleaning is finished only when someone else can see what you did, why, and what it means for the results, and can repeat it. Learn to write a data quality report, keep a cleaning log, and run a reproducible workflow from the raw export to analysis-ready data.
x: Data quality report Raw data Cleaning log Reproducibility Data lineage Percentage point Data minimisation Pseudonymised Explain who reads a data quality report and what each reader needs from it. Write the sections of a data quality report, including each issue, the decision taken and its rationale, and the limitations that remain. Calculate before-and-after profile figures and describe how exclusions change who the data represent. Construct a reproducible cleaning workflow that keeps the raw data untouched and records its lineage. Evaluate reporting choices for honesty, bias and the protection of personal data.

t: The marketing mix and customer value
s: M02 · Marketing turns an idea into an offer that people choose over the alternatives. Learn what customer value is, how product, price, place and promotion each create or capture it, and how to test whether a plan’s four decisions fit each other and the customers they are meant for.
x: Marketing Customer value Target market Positioning Value proposition Marketing mix 4Ps 4Cs 7Ps Explain what marketing is and what customer value means, in your own words and in the American Marketing Association’s. Classify marketing decisions as product, price, place or promotion decisions. Analyse whether the four decisions in a plan are consistent with each other and with the target market and positioning. Calculate how a price and a channel together determine what a business keeps per unit, and what a customer gives up to buy. Compare the 4Ps with the 4Cs and the 7Ps, and describe how the mix differs between business and consumer markets.

s: M02 · A product is a bundle of benefits, not just a thing. Learn to analyse an offer by its levels and attributes, classify it by how people buy it, describe a company’s product lines, and work out what quality and range decisions cost, using Lantern Cold Brew’s liquid, flavours and can.
x: Product Core benefit Actual product Augmented product Brand Packaging Convenience product Shopping product Specialty product Unsought product Product line Product mix Product mix width Product line length Product line depth Product mix consistency Line extension Distinguish the core benefit, the actual product and the augmented product of an offer. Classify consumer products as convenience, shopping, specialty or unsought products, and explain what each class implies for price, place and promotion. Describe a company’s product mix by its width, line length, depth and consistency, and explain line stretching, line filling and line extension. Calculate the cost consequences of quality and range decisions, including the cost-of-goods difference between tiers and the extra listing fees of a wider range. Evaluate a product decision against the positioning, the other three Ps and the costs it creates.

s: M02 · Products, like markets, tend to be born, grow, mature and fade, and each stage asks for a different mix. Learn the stages, the decisions that typically fit each one, how to read a product’s stage from data, and why the life cycle is a planning hypothesis rather than a law.
x: Product life cycle Introduction stage Growth stage Maturity stage Decline stage Style Fashion Fad Describe the four stages of the product life cycle and the typical sales, profit, customers and competition in each. Choose objectives and 4P decisions that fit a product’s stage, and explain when the typical prescription would not fit. Distinguish the life cycles of a product category, a product form and a brand, and of styles, fashions and fads. Calculate year-on-year growth and seasonally adjusted sales, and use them to judge which stage a product is in. Evaluate ways to extend a mature product’s life, and assess the criticisms of the life-cycle concept.

s: M02 · Price is the only part of the mix that brings money in. Learn to separate fixed from variable costs, work with contribution, markups and margins, find the break-even volume, and set a price between the floor your costs set and the ceiling your customers’ alternatives set.
x: Fixed cost Variable cost Contribution margin Break-even point Cost-plus pricing Markup Margin Target-return pricing Value-based pricing Competition-based pricing Price floor Price ceiling Classify costs as fixed or variable and calculate the contribution margin per unit and as a ratio of price. Convert between a markup on cost and a margin on price, and set the price that achieves a target margin. Calculate the break-even volume, the break-even revenue and the volume needed for a target profit. Apply cost-plus, target-return, value-based and competition-based pricing, and explain what each one leaves out. Identify a product’s price floor and price ceiling and use them, with competitors’ prices, to judge a proposed price.
